claims.text: Nanoscale platinum-group-metal catalysts exhibit exceptional activity, selectivity, and durability in ethanol oxidation.
Their ethanol-oxidation performance is primarily governed by a dynamically strained surface.
Surface strain tunes the d-band center so as to optimize adsorption and transformation of reaction intermediates.
The as-synthesized catalyst has high surface strain and defect density.
Annealing at 300 °C for one hour under inert atmosphere will relax the catalyst's surface strain.
Complete ethanol oxidation proceeds through a 12-electron and 12-proton pathway.
Surface strain is associated with the position of the catalyst's d-band center.
Surface strain and d-band-center position can be measured using operando XPS and EXAFS.
An optimally positioned d-band center enables balanced adsorption of critical reaction intermediates.
Annealing-induced strain relaxation shifts the d-band center away from its optimum.
The shifted d-band center weakens the catalyst's ability to stabilize intermediates required for complete ethanol oxidation.
The as-synthesized high-strain catalyst will have a higher ethanol-oxidation turnover frequency than the annealed catalyst.
The as-synthesized high-strain catalyst will show greater selectivity toward complete oxidation and CO2 production.
The as-synthesized high-strain catalyst will be more durable than the annealed catalyst.
Annealing will cause an approximately 30% decrease in catalytic activity and selectivity.
The performance decrease after annealing will be accompanied by a detectable d-band-center shift.
Morphological changes caused by annealing would confound attribution of performance changes solely to strain.
Prior PGM-catalyst observations support a relationship between optimized surface electronic structure, a shifted d-band center, and enhanced catalytic activity.
